An indirect question is a question "hidden" inside a sentence: after "je me demande, je ne sais pas, dites-moi, il m’a demandé, savez-vous…". The golden rule: the word order becomes NORMAL (subject + verb), with no inversion, no "est-ce que" and no question mark (unless the main sentence is a question).
Je me demande si les enfants viendront.
Je ne sais pas où est l’école. / où l’école est.
When the answer would be "yes" or "no", the indirect question is introduced by SI (if / whether). "Si" + "il / ils" becomes "s’il / s’ils":
She wants to know whether the lessons are free.
I’ll ask him whether he’d agree.

Don’t translate "if / whether" with "que"! "Je me demande que…" is wrong. And don’t use the future after a conditional "si" — but after an INTERROGATIVE "si" the future is correct: "Je me demande s’il viendra."
3. Qu’est-ce qui → ce qui, qu’est-ce que → ce que
For "what?" the form changes. It’s the main trap of the chapter:
Je ne sais pas ce que les parents penseront.
Demandez-lui ce dont il a besoin.
"Que / quoi" alone don’t appear in indirect questions: "Je ne sais pas que faire" is a fixed exception (with the infinitive) = I don’t know what to do.
Où, quand, comment, pourquoi, combien, qui, quel / quelle stay the same:
I don’t know how they’ll react.
I wonder how many violins are sleeping in attics.
She asked me which day the children should come.
5. In the past: sequence of tenses
As with reported speech (ch. 38), if the main verb is in the past, the tenses shift:
si les cours étaient gratuits (present → imperfect)
si nous avions survécu (passé composé → pluperfect)

The day after she got back from Romania, Hélène gathered the residents in the common room. Everyone wanted to know how the trip had gone. Madame Lambert had prepared a list of questions, written in her beautiful schoolteacher’s handwriting, and she asked them one by one, like an exam.

She asked whether the plane had been comfortable, how long the journey had taken, what people ate over there and whether Romanians spoke French. Hélène answered everything patiently. Monsieur Petit, for his part, only wanted to know whether Romanian postmen had bicycles or cars.

Then Hélène told them about the hora. She explained how everyone held hands, how she had stood up despite Odile, and what she had felt in the middle of the circle. "I still wonder how I did it," she said. "I think my legs were twenty years old that evening."

Then she took the embroidered ie out of her wardrobe and passed it from hand to hand. The residents touched it carefully, like a museum piece. Madame Lambert wanted to know who had embroidered it and how long it had taken. Nobody knew the answer, but everyone agreed: months.

It was at that moment that Julien came in, a little out of breath. He had just seen Monsieur Garnier. He explained the orchestra project, the problem with the instruments, the idea of the collection. Then he asked, rather shyly, whether any of them had an instrument forgotten at the back of a cupboard.

There was a silence. Then a small lady at the back of the room raised her hand. It was Madame Roux, who hardly ever spoke. "I have a clarinet," she said. "My husband’s. He played in the Villeurbanne brass band. I wonder whether it still works. It hasn’t been used for forty years."

It was like a signal. Monsieur Petit said he had a harmonica, a present from his colleagues at the post office. A former butcher announced that he had a drum, without being able to explain why. Madame Lambert confessed that she had kept the recorder from her 1978 class, with which she used to torture her pupils.

On Saturday 2 September, at nine in the morning, there was already a queue outside Monsieur Garnier’s shop. Elderly people with dusty cases, parents with children’s guitars, a young man carrying a double bass on his back like a giant rucksack.

Monsieur Garnier wrote everything down in a big notebook: the donor’s name, the instrument, its condition. Julien and Radu helped carry things. Lucia tried out the guitars. Ioana, with Rose-Hélène in the baby carrier, served coffee and croissants donated by Sophie, the baker, who had asked whether she could help too.

Around eleven, a very elegant lady arrived by taxi. She asked to see the person in charge. The driver took a black leather case out of the boot. Inside was a magnificent cello, made of an almost red wood. Monsieur Garnier went quite pale. "Madame, I don’t know whether you realise what you’re giving me."

The lady smiled. She explained that it was her son’s cello. He had studied at the Conservatoire thirty years ago, then he had become a doctor and had never played again. He now lived in Canada. "I asked him what he wanted me to do with it," she said. "He answered: give it to a child who dreams of it."

In the afternoon, Hélène arrived with Odile and half the care home, in the home’s minibus. Madame Roux was holding her clarinet against her chest. She put it on the table very slowly. Then she asked Julien whether she might, one day, hear the child who would play it.

Julien promised her she would be in the front row at the first concert. Madame Roux nodded. Then she added, in a trembling voice: "My husband’s name was Lucien. He played out of tune, but he played with his heart. Tell the child to play with their heart." Julien had to turn away for a moment.

In the evening, when the shop had closed, Monsieur Garnier counted: forty-seven instruments. Twelve violins, half of which needed new strings, six flutes, three clarinets, four guitars, two trumpets, a drum, a harmonica, a double bass, a very valuable cello and fifteen other objects that nobody could quite identify.

Among these mysterious objects was a kind of small wooden harp, with metal strings. Nobody knew where it came from or who had brought it. Lucia examined it for a long time. "I wonder whether it isn’t an instrument from Eastern Europe," she said. "Radu, do you know what it is?"

Radu’s eyes widened. "It’s a țambal! A small țambal, like the village musicians have!" He struck a string with a pencil, and a clear, slightly metallic sound filled the shop. Everyone wondered how a Romanian instrument could have ended up in a shop in Lyon.

Monsieur Garnier leafed through his notebook. On the corresponding line there was only a first name, written in a clumsy hand: "Mihaela". No surname, no address, no phone number. He didn’t remember the person. In the morning crush, someone must have left it without waiting.

Ioana took a photo of the instrument and sent it to her grandmother. The answer came an hour later, through her mother’s voice on the phone: "Buni says it’s a țambal from Moldavia, very old. She wants to know who gave it, and why." Ioana replied that she was wondering the same thing.

That evening, on the way home, Julien looked at the list of forty-seven instruments. He wondered how many stories were hidden behind each of them: a brass band in Villeurbanne, a son in Canada, a class of 1978, an unknown Mihaela. "It’s not instruments they’ve given us," he told Ioana. "It’s memories."

Ioana smiled. She wondered whether, one day, someone would give the piano from rue d’Austerlitz to a child who dreamed of it. And whether that child would find, in an old envelope, two waltzes and two little papers with the same word. Then she told herself that was a question for a very long time from now.

On Sunday, Monsieur Garnier took the instruments to his luthier friends, in a tiny workshop on the slopes of the Croix-Rousse. The two old craftsmen examined everything in silence, nodding. Then the elder asked Julien how much time he was giving them. "Three weeks," Julien replied. The luthier sighed: "I wonder why musicians are always in a hurry."

He nevertheless promised that the violins would be ready for the first rehearsal. The țambal, on the other hand, he refused to touch. "That one, I don’t know who made it, or how you tune it," he confessed. "You’d have to ask someone who knows." Radu smiled: he knew exactly whom to ask.

The following Monday, Julien went to the school in La Duchère to meet the children. There were thirty of them, sitting on the floor in the covered playground, and they looked at him suspiciously. A ten-year-old boy in the front row raised his hand before he had even said hello. "Sir, is it true we’ll be allowed to touch the violins?"

Julien smiled. He opened the black leather case and took out the cello made of almost red wood. Thirty pairs of eyes widened at the same time. "Not only will you be allowed to touch them," he said. "But I wonder which of you will be the first to play in front of Madame Roux." The boy’s name was Yanis. He was the first to stand up.
